claims.claim: Labeling theory, also called the social reaction perspective, shifts the explanatory question from the causes of an initial rule violation to the consequences of society's reaction to it, and it deliberately does not attempt to explain the first offense.

Frank Tannenbaum's Crime and the Community (1938) described a process in which a community's judgment shifts from the act to the young person who committed it; he called the process of defining, identifying, segregating and making the youth self-conscious about being bad 'tagging', and the surrounding community drama the 'dramatization of evil', arguing that the process itself produces further delinquency.

Edwin Lemert's Social Pathology (1951) introduced the distinction between primary deviance - initial rule-breaking that is rationalized or otherwise absorbed into a socially acceptable role - and secondary deviance, which a person adopts as a means of defense, attack or adjustment to the problems created by other people's reaction. Lemert deliberately did not theorize the causes of primary deviance, leaving those to other criminological theories.

Howard Becker's Outsiders (1963) argued that deviance is not a quality of the act a person commits but a consequence of the application by others of rules and sanctions, so that the deviant is the person to whom the label has successfully been applied.

Becker described moral entrepreneurs of two kinds - rule-creators, who campaign to have a rule made because they see an evil requiring prohibition, and rule-enforcers, who are interested in enforcing existing rules and justifying their work and who therefore develop their own priorities about which rules and which offenders to pursue. This is the source of the labeling tradition's interest in differential enforcement.

Becker argued that the label 'criminal' is so stigmatizing in American society that it becomes a master status, overriding any other role or position the labeled person holds, and he outlined a deviant career whose third phase is movement into a deviant group that supplies rationalizations, motives and attitudes supporting further deviance.

Erving Goffman's Stigma: Notes on the Management of Spoiled Identity (1963) defined stigma as a deeply discrediting attribute that reduces its bearer, in the eyes of others, from a whole and usual person to a tainted, discounted one.
Later sociological work refined stigma into the co-occurrence of labeling, stereotyping, separation, status loss and discrimination, and held that stigmatization requires the exercise of power.

Labeling theory declined in the second half of the 1970s under criticism that not everyone labeled goes on to offend more (deterrence research showed punishment sometimes reduces reoffending), that the theory ignored individual differences in response to labels, and that it offered no workable account of how society should respond to crime; Charles Wellford's 1975 assessment in Social Problems is the standard critical citation.

Bernburg and Krohn (2003), using the Rochester Youth Development Study panel of 605 males followed over nine years, found that official intervention by police or the juvenile justice system reduced the chance of graduating high school, which in turn reduced employment and raised the risk of adult offending; effects were stronger for lower-class and African American males, and a direct effect of intervention on adult offending remained after controlling for education and employment.

Bernburg, Krohn and Rivera (2006), using three waves of the same Rochester panel, found that juvenile justice intervention predicted later involvement in deviant social groups - street gangs and delinquent peers - and that serious subsequent delinquency was mediated through that involvement, with a direct effect of intervention also remaining.

Gatti, Tremblay and Vitaro (2009), using a Montreal community sample of 779 low-socioeconomic-status boys, found that at the same level of self-reported antisocial behavior, boys who were poor, impulsive, poorly supervised and exposed to deviant friends were more likely to be processed by the juvenile court, that court intervention was associated with greatly increased likelihood of penal system involvement in adulthood, and that dispositions involving placement had the most negative association.

The Campbell systematic review by Petrosino, Turpin-Petrosino and Guckenburg (2010) synthesized 29 eligible controlled trials covering 7,304 juveniles reported between 1973 and 2008 and concluded that formal juvenile system processing does not have a crime control effect: almost all results ran in the negative direction across prevalence, incidence, severity and self-report outcomes, and comparisons against diversion programs produced larger negative effect sizes than comparisons against doing nothing.

John Braithwaite's Crime, Shame and Reintegration (1989) distinguished reintegrative shaming - disapproval expressed within a continuum of respect for the person, followed by words, gestures or ceremonies that return the person to the community of the law-abiding - from stigmatizing or disintegrative shaming, which treats the person as bad and is unforgiving, and predicted lower crime rates where shaming is reintegrative and higher rates where it is stigmatizing.

Braithwaite's distinction allows both the labeling prediction and the deterrence prediction to be partly correct, because it makes the effect of a sanction depend on the form the sanction takes rather than on its existence.

U.S. juvenile diversion is explicitly grounded in labeling theory: OJJDP's Model Programs Guide literature review names labeling theory (citing Becker 1963) and differential association as the two theoretical rationales for diversion, and NIJ's CrimeSolutions practice profile for juvenile diversion makes the same attribution and cites Petrosino and colleagues (2010) as supporting evidence.

The evidence on juvenile diversion outcomes is mixed rather than settled: OJJDP's review reports one meta-analysis of 28 studies finding diversion's effect on recidivism nonsignificant and no better than traditional processing, and another of 45 studies finding significantly lower recidivism for diverted youths; CrimeSolutions rates the practice Promising rather than Effective.

Record sealing and expungement, and fair-chance or ban-the-box hiring rules that restrict when employers may ask about criminal history, are documented U.S. responses to the collateral consequences that follow a conviction.

Observational findings that formally processed youths fare worse do not by themselves establish that processing caused the difference, because assignment to formal processing is not random and the characteristics that make formal handling more likely can independently predict later offending; this is why the experimental evidence synthesized in the Campbell review carries more weight.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does official sanction increase or decrease subsequent offending?
positions: Labeling theory predicts that formal intervention stigmatizes, narrows legitimate opportunity, and increases subsequent offending.

Deterrence research finds that sanction risk - especially the certainty of being caught - can reduce offending, and 1970s critics used this to argue labeling theory had no room for a well-documented effect.
Braithwaite's position is that both can be right, because the effect depends on whether shaming is reintegrative or stigmatizing.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states all three positions and attributes each. It reports NIJ's summary that certainty of apprehension deters more than severity and that imprisonment is not an effective deterrent, and it presents Braithwaite's distinction as the reconciling move rather than as a settled finding.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How strong is the empirical support for labeling theory?
positions: 1970s critics, including Wellford (1975), argued the empirical support was weak and that the theory said nothing about the origin of primary deviance.

Post-2000 longitudinal work (Bernburg and Krohn 2003; Bernburg, Krohn and Rivera 2006; Gatti, Tremblay and Vitaro 2009) and the Campbell review of controlled trials (Petrosino et al. 2010) find formal system contact associated with, and in the experimental subset followed by, worse subsequent outcomes.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states both explicitly and does not resolve them in the theory's favor. It says the modern evidence supports the association between formal system contact and worse later outcomes more strongly than it isolates 'the label' as the operating mechanism, and it notes that the tested mediators - schooling, employment, deviant peers - never account for the whole effect.

positions: Schwalbe and colleagues (2012), as summarized by OJJDP, found across 28 studies that diversion's effect on recidivism was nonsignificant and no better than traditional processing.
Wilson and Hoge (2012), as summarized by OJJDP, found across 45 studies that diverted youths had significantly lower average recidivism than comparison youths.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the disagreement as reported by OJJDP and CrimeSolutions, notes the Promising (not Effective) rating, and states explicitly that evaluating diversion policy is not this lesson's job.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Wording of Goffman's definition of stigma
positions: The National Academies 2016 report renders Goffman's definition as a 'deeply discrediting attitude'.
The standard rendering of Goffman's 1963 text is 'an attribute that is deeply discrediting'.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses 'attribute', which matches the sense of the surrounding quoted clause the National Academies report reproduces ('from a whole and usual person to a tainted, discounted one') and the standard scholarly rendering. Goffman's book itself was not read for this lesson; the definition is carried on the National Academies report.
